title: Impact-resistant, autonomous robots inspired by tensegrity architecture - Nature Machine Intelligence
text:
AbstractTensegrity robots—composed of rigid struts suspended in a network of elastic cables—have been proposed as the next generation of planetary rovers and disaster response platforms, with their inherent impact resilience potentially eliminating the need for separate landers if they can survive aerial deployment. Although non-robotic tensegrity structures have demonstrated substantial impact resistance, integrating this property into autonomous robotic systems remains a grand challenge. Here we present Tribar, a three-bar tensegrity robot capable of surviving high-impact landings (at least 5.7 m) and autonomously navigating unstructured terrain post impact. We characterize the robot’s locomotion, evaluate its autonomous navigation capabilities, benchmark its performance relative to state-of-the-art tensegrity robots and demonstrate its robustness through successful locomotion after a cliff fall.

Data availability

All data necessary to interpret, verify and extend the research in this Article are available via Figshare at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.32273583 (ref. 54).
Code availability

The custom code used to control the tensegrity robot during the experiments described in this study is available via GitHub at https://github.com/ChemStud24/tensegrity-control and archived via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20347612 (ref. 55). A physical tensegrity robot is required to run the code; however, the source code is still provided as a reference for the implementation of the control policies and algorithms described in the Article.
